records.text: The Bayesian rule is the most important formula in machine learning.
The lecture on Linear Models and Intro to Deep Learning builds on the Bayesian rule.
Given a hypothesis θ and evidence D, the posterior p(θ|D) is given by p(θ|D) = p(D|θ)p(θ)/p(D).
The prior p(θ) is what we believe before seeing data.
The likelihood p(D|θ) is how probable the observed data is under a given hypothesis.
The posterior p(θ|D) is our updated belief after seeing evidence.
The evidence (marginal likelihood) p(D) is a normalising constant.
Maximum likelihood (ML) is defined as θ_ML = argmax_θ p(D|θ) and is purely frequentist with no prior.
Maximum a posteriori (MAP) is defined as θ_MAP = argmax_θ p(θ|D) ∝ p(D|θ)p(θ) and incorporates a prior.
Full posterior inference and the predictive distribution p(x|D) follow from the Bayesian identity.
In deep learning practice, the loss function is almost always of the form −(log p(D|θ) + log p(θ)).
Minimising this loss function yields the MAP estimate θ_MAP.
θ_MAP is a point estimate, specifically the maximum of the posterior distribution.
The model’s uncertainty is captured by the full posterior distribution.
For huge neural networks, we are usually forced to settle for the point estimate θ_MAP instead of using the full posterior.
Classical probability, defined as the frequency limit of experiments, works for repeatable events.
In machine learning, we often need to reason about unique events such as Spain winning the 2026 World Cup, whether the Odyssey was written by a woman, or AGI risk by 2030.
In these cases, probability functions as a degree of belief, representing our uncertainty.
Both interpretations of probability follow the same mathematical rules.
When we train a model, we are not reaching a logical certainty; we are updating our beliefs.
Even with vast data, the result of training remains a distribution.
The best we typically get from that distribution is a point estimate.
That point estimate should be interpreted cautiously.
Understanding which quantity is on which side of the conditioning bar is essential.
Many real‑world mistakes come from swapping the quantities on the sides of the conditioning bar.
In the two children problem, a person has two children, and each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl independently.
When you ask 'Do you have any boys?' and the answer is 'yes', the sample space is BB, BG, GB, GG, each with prior probability 1/4.
Eliminating GG leaves three equally likely cases.
Two of those three cases contain a girl.
Therefore, P(has a girl | has a boy) = 2/3.
When you meet one of the children and it is a boy, you have fixed one specific child.
This eliminates two cases; for example, if the met child is the first, only BB and BG remain.
Thus, P(other is girl) = 1/2.
This demonstrates that the nature of the evidence changes the conditional probability even though both times you learn that there is a boy.
A rare blood type with 1% prevalence is found at the crime scene, and the defendant also has it.
The prosecutor's fallacy is: 'The chance of having this blood type if innocent is 1%, therefore the defendant is guilty with probability 99%'.
The prosecutor's fallacy equates P(blood type | innocent) with P(innocent | blood type).
Correct inference requires the prior probability of guilt, the base rate of the blood type, and other factors.
The defence attorney's error is: 'A million people live in the city, so ≈10,000 have the same blood type; the evidence gives only a 0.01% probability of guilt.'
The defence attorney implicitly assumes that among those 10,000 everyone is equally likely to be the killer.
The defence attorney ignores why the defendant is on trial.
In the O.J. Simpson case, the defence argued that only 1 in 2500 women subjected to domestic violence is murdered, therefore domestic violence is irrelevant.
The defence confused P(murdered | history of violence) with P(husband is murderer | woman murdered AND history of violence).
Using the same statistics, the correct estimate is around 7/8, meaning the husband is by far the most likely perpetrator.
The court's acceptance of the defence's argument was a Bayesian mistake.
Always ask yourself what is on the left and right of the conditioning bar, i.e., what exactly you are trying to estimate.
A linear model assumes the target y is a linear combination of input features.
The linear model is expressed as y(x,w) = w^T φ(x).
φ(x) is a feature vector that may be non‑linear.
By prepending a constant feature φ_0(x) = 1, the intercept is absorbed into the weight vector, which is a standard trick to keep formulas clean.
Given a training set of N data points (x_n, t_n), the goal is to find the best weight vector w.
Minimizing the sum of squared errors (RSS) is the usual choice for finding the best w.
Minimizing RSS is not arbitrary; it follows from a probabilistic model.
Assumption 1 for the linear model: The data points are conditionally independent given the parameters.
Assumption 2: The centre of the noise distribution is the linear function itself: E[t_n] = w^T φ(x_n).
Assumption 3: The noise is zero-mean Gaussian with constant variance σ^2, so p(t_n | x_n, w, σ^2) = N(t_n | w^T φ(x_n), σ^2).
The Gaussian noise is natural because of the central limit theorem, as many small independent perturbations sum to an approximately normal distribution.
Assumption 4 (hidden): Homoscedasticity – the noise variance σ^2 is the same for all data points.
Homoscedasticity allows pulling σ out of the sum in the likelihood.
If the variance changes, the loss function must be modified, which is one reason to understand the assumptions.
The log-likelihood for linear regression under Gaussian noise is ln p(t|X,w,σ^2) = -(N/2)ln(2πσ^2) - (1/(2σ^2))Σ (t_n - w^T φ_n)^2.
Maximising this log-likelihood with respect to w is equivalent to minimising the RSS.
The square error directly reflects the Gaussian noise assumption.
To illustrate overfitting, consider a one-dimensional input x and a true function that is a sine wave.
A polynomial of degree 1 (straight line) under-fits the sine wave.
A polynomial of degree 3 already captures the sine wave’s single bump well.
A polynomial of degree 10 with only 11 training points passes through every training point exactly (RSS = 0) but oscillates wildly between points, which is the classic picture of overfitting.
In high dimensions, overfitting arises naturally when expanding features.
Going from D original features to quadratic features gives approximately D^2/2 new features, including cross-terms x_i x_j.
If D=100, the number of features jumps to about 5000.
Many of these new features are irrelevant, but it is not known a priori which ones.
Therefore, all features must be included, making overfitting almost inevitable.
A symptom of overfitting is that validation or test error grows while training error stays tiny.
Another symptom is that the model coefficients explode, for example reaching ±50 when the inputs and outputs are on the order of 1.
The explosion of coefficients is a sign that the model is using unreasonable parameter values to exactly fit noise.
In a high-dimensional weight space, the model has too much variety.
Constraining the weights toward zero reduces the effective complexity of the model.
Regularization is equivalent to placing a prior on the parameters.
We want the prior distribution p(w) to be concentrated near zero to express the belief that extremely large weights are unlikely.
A natural choice for such a prior is a Gaussian distribution: p(w) = N(w | 0, (1/α)I).
The MAP objective is obtained by adding the log-prior to the log-likelihood.
The MAP objective for linear regression with a Gaussian prior is -(1/(2σ^2))Σ (t_n - w^T φ_n)^2 - (α/2) w^T w + constant.
This is exactly ridge regression (L2 regularization).
The hyperparameter α trades off data fit against weight size.
L2 regularization does not change the number of parameters.
L2 regularization pulls the solution toward the origin within the fixed-dimensional weight space.
Using a Laplace prior p(w_j) ∝ e^{-α|w_j|} results in the L1 (LASSO) regularizer Σ |w_j|.
LASSO drives many coefficients exactly to zero, producing sparse models.
Sparse models are useful for automatic feature selection from a large pool of candidates.
The probabilistic view explains why loss functions in any model, including deep neural networks, can be seen as derived from a likelihood and a prior.
The regularizer is the part of the loss function that does not depend on the data.
Regularization operates within a fixed model, i.e., with a fixed set of parameters.
Model selection, using criteria like AIC or BIC, chooses between models of different complexity by approximating the evidence p(D|M_k).
Regularization and model selection are separate levels.
A classifier that directly outputs class labels (e.g., 0/1 threshold) has zero gradient almost everywhere.
Such a classifier provides no learning signal for earlier layers.
We want a probability distribution over classes to express uncertainty.
For binary classification, we want to model p(C1|x) in a way that allows a linear relationship somewhere.
Bayes’ theorem gives p(C1|x) = p(x|C1)p(C1) / (p(x|C1)p(C1) + p(x|C2)p(C2)).
The odds are defined as p(C1)/p(C2).
The log-odds (logit) is defined as a = ln( (p(x|C1)p(C1)) / (p(x|C2)p(C2)) ).
The logit a can be any real number, so it can be modelled as a linear function a = w^T φ(x).
Inverting the logit transformation gives the logistic sigmoid: σ(a) = 1/(1+e^{-a}).
This sigmoid function maps the linear combination to a probability p(C1|x).
The logistic sigmoid σ(a) is S-shaped.
σ(a) saturates at 0 and 1.
σ(a) passes through 0.5 at a=0.
σ(a) provides a smooth interpolation that is differentiable everywhere.
For binary classification with targets in {0,1}, the likelihood is p(t|w) = Π y_n^{t_n} (1-y_n)^{1-t_n} where y_n = σ(w^T φ_n).
Taking negative log gives the cross-entropy error: E(w) = -Σ [t_n ln y_n + (1-t_n) ln(1-y_n)].
Minimising this cross-entropy error fits the logistic regression model.
The optimum can be found by gradient descent.
For multi-class classification with K classes, a vector of scores a_k = w_k^T x is used.
The softmax function defines p(C_k|x) = e^{a_k} / Σ_j e^{a_j}.
The name 'softmax' reflects that it softly picks the maximum score; when one a_k dominates, the output is nearly a one-hot vector.
The scores can be any real numbers; because of the exponential, adding a constant to all a_k leaves the probabilities unchanged, so negative values are harmless.
For a one-hot target vector, the loss reduces to the negative log-probability of the correct class.
In a deep neural network for classification, the main body of the network extracts features z of dimension D.
The last layer is often a linear transformation Wz (a K×D matrix) giving scores, followed by softmax to produce a probability vector.
Thus the final stage is exactly logistic regression on the learned features; all previous layers are doing feature extraction for this linear classifier.
For regression tasks, the last layer is analogously a linear layer (no softmax) on top of the extracted features.
The human brain contains roughly 10^11 neurons.
Each neuron makes approximately 7000 synaptic connections.
The total number of parameters (synaptic connections) is roughly between 10^14 and 10^15.
A neuron receives inputs through dendrites, which can number in the thousands per neuron.
The neuron integrates its inputs via weighted connections at synapses.
When sufficiently excited, the neuron sends out a spike along its axon.
Spikes are all-or-nothing events.
Information is coded in the firing rate, which is between 10 and 200 Hz.
The brain is a massively parallel but shallow computer.
It can perform a huge number of operations simultaneously.
A single pass through the whole visual system takes only 200–300 ms, which corresponds to just a few tens of sequential steps.
Deep artificial networks are wide and use relatively few (hundreds, not thousands) of layer-wise transformations.
The brain exhibits neuroplasticity, adapting to completely new sensory modalities such as seeing via a tongue electrode grid.
This neuroplasticity suggests the existence of a single, general learning algorithm in the brain.
The idea of a general learning algorithm motivates artificial neural networks.
A large composition of simple, identical units can learn a vast variety of functions.
In 1943, McCulloch and Pitts proposed a mathematical model of a neuron as a weighted sum followed by a threshold.
This model is essentially the modern artificial neuron.
In 1948, Alan Turing sketched the idea of multilayer networks.
In 1958, Rosenblatt built the Perceptron.
The Perceptron is a single neuron trained by gradient descent.
The Perceptron could recognise letters.
The Perceptron was hailed in the press as the first step to general AI.
In 1969, Minsky and Papert showed that a single perceptron cannot solve the XOR problem because the classes are not linearly separable.
The finding that a single perceptron cannot solve XOR only proves that one neuron is insufficient.
A network of perceptrons can easily solve XOR.
The result contributed to the first "AI winter".
In the 1970s-80s, backpropagation (applying the chain rule through the network) was independently rediscovered multiple times.
Backpropagation makes it possible to train multilayer perceptrons.
Deep networks appeared in the 1980s, including convolutional nets and recurrent nets.
In the 1990s, neural networks fell out of favour because they underperformed specialised models on small datasets and limited hardware.
The slogan was: "neural networks are the second best way of doing just about anything."
In 2006, Hinton's group revived deep learning with unsupervised pretraining and GPU acceleration.
GPUs provided a 10–20× speedup.
The speedup moved computations from "not working" to "working".
In the 2010s, deep nets revolutionised speech recognition (e.g., Siri).
In the 2010s, deep nets revolutionised computer vision (e.g., AlexNet in 2012).
In the 2010s, deep nets revolutionised NLP.
By 2017, the Transformer architecture arrived.
The Transformer reshaped the whole field again.
The basic unit of deep networks is an artificial neuron, defined by $$y = h\!\left(\sum_i w_i x_i\right) = h(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}).$$
The weights w are the learnable parameters.
The activation function h must be non-linear.
If the activation function is linear, a composition of linear transforms remains linear.
If the activation function is linear, a deep network collapses to a single linear layer.
Any non-linearity suffices to achieve universal approximation.
Typically, neurons are arranged in layers.
The output of one layer becomes the input to the next layer.
Connectionism is the idea that a huge composition of extremely simple units yields an extraordinarily complex function.
Connectionism is the core idea of deep learning.
The key challenge in deep learning is training, i.e., finding all weights via gradient descent.
Training requires computing gradients through the whole computational graph.
Backpropagation computes gradients through the computational graph.
The next lecture will cover gradient descent variants and backpropagation.
For complicated non-convex functions, the only feasible optimisation method is gradient descent.
Gradient descent repeatedly moves a small step opposite to the gradient ∇_w E(w).
Gradient descent finds a local minimum.
There is never a guarantee that gradient descent finds the global minimum.
Even for logistic regression, a closed-form solution does not exist.
Iterative gradient methods are mandatory for logistic regression.
Iterative gradient methods are mandatory for all neural networks.
